posts.quote: A JUDGE JUST GAGGED A CABINET SECRETARY OVER AN EASTER EMAIL THAT SAID "HE IS RISEN."
posts.alt: Official portrait photo of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins smiling in front of an American flag and the USDA seal. Text below reads: A judge just gagged a Cabinet secretary over an Easter email that said "He is risen."
posts.caption:
A federal judge has told a Cabinet secretary what she can say to her own employees.

On November 19, Judge Trina Thompson of the Northern District of California granted a preliminary injunction limiting the religious messages Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins sends to USDA staff. The lawsuit came after an Easter email on April 5 that said "He is risen," which went to about 100,000 employees, and a Christmas message sent on December 23.

Thompson wrote that the messages "go too far" and "suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." She also said "the good faith intentions of the Secretary are not the issue here."

The order does not stop Rollins from sharing her faith. It stops her from using her position to pressure the people who work for her. The judge threw out the Administrative Procedure Act claims but kept the constitutional claim alive.
posts.first:
USDA fired back, calling the case "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary," according to AP. The agency is weighing an appeal.

Here is the real question. Two holiday emails, one on Easter and one at Christmas, now sit at the center of a federal court fight over the Establishment Clause. Supporters of the secretary say a greeting is not a command. The employees who sued, backed by a union with more than 19,000 members, say a message from the boss is never just a greeting.

Whichever way an appeals court goes, this one is going to be argued for a long time.

One detail stands out. The judge said Rollins's good intentions were not the issue. That is the whole fight in a sentence: what a secretary means by a greeting versus how it lands on an employee who answers to her. That is the line the courts are now being asked to draw.

posts.quote: MAMDANI SAYS RIKERS CLOSES "ONCE AND FOR ALL." THE BILL: ABOUT $16 BILLION. THE DEADLINE: 5 YEARS LATE.
posts.alt: Photo-style AI image of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaking at a press conference in front of microphones. Text below reads: Mamdani says Rikers closes "once and for all." The bill: about $16 billion. The deadline: 5 years late.
posts.caption:
New York's mayor says Rikers Island will finally close. The timeline and the price tag tell a different story.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on November 20 that the jail will close by 2032, replaced by four smaller borough jails. Brooklyn is slated for 2029, the Bronx and Queens for 2031, and Manhattan for 2032. "It is time to finally close Rikers Island," he said.

The city's own law required Rikers to close by 2027. AP reports the city is "all but certain" to miss that deadline, which puts the new date about five years late.

The population is the next problem. Roughly 6,000 people are held at Rikers today, and the plan targets about 4,500. Daily Wire reports the project's cost has grown from about $8.7 billion to about $16 billion. Other outlets cite lower figures, and Breitbart notes Mamdani has not named a funding source.
posts.first:
Reading the plan closely, it depends on a lot of things going right. The jail population has to drop by roughly a quarter. Four new jails have to be built on schedule, in boroughs where neighbors have fought every one of them. And the money has to come from somewhere.

In the meantime, more than 50 people have died in custody at Rikers since 2022. Even supporters of closing the jail say the city needs a backup plan if the buildings run late.

Everyone agrees Rikers has been a disaster. A plan that misses its legal deadline by five years, costs nearly double the first estimate and has no named funding source is a different thing than a plan that works.

posts.quote: A SECOND JUDGE JUST FROZE TRUMP'S ARCH. HER REASON: NO CONGRESSIONAL APPROVAL.
posts.alt: Two panels. Left: a photo of the road and stone gate pillar at Memorial Circle near Arlington, Virginia. Right: an official portrait photo of President Donald Trump in a blue suit and red tie. Text below reads: A second judge just froze Trump's arch. Her reason: no congressional approval.
posts.caption:
President Trump's planned triumphal arch just lost a second round in federal court.

On November 20, Judge Leonie Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia granted an injunction blocking construction. The suit was filed October 8 by the Arlington County Board. According to Politico, she told the government: "You don't have congressional approval for this project." The order has no expiration date.

It is the second judge to step in. Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington blocked construction on November 6, and that order was extended to December 3.

The arch is planned for Memorial Circle, at the Virginia end of Memorial Bridge. The Justice Department said it will appeal.
posts.first:
Supporters argue Congress approved a monument at the site more than a century ago, and that the planning commission has already voted its approval. Judges so far have not agreed that this is enough for a project of this size.

For the White House, the timing matters. Every week the arch sits in court is another week without construction, and two federal courts in two jurisdictions now stand in the way. Chutkan sits in the District of Columbia and Brinkema in Virginia, so the arch is now tied up on both sides of the Potomac. The injunction from Virginia has no end date, which means the administration cannot simply wait out a short pause the way it might with a two-week order.

Expect an appeal. Whether an appeals court sees the old congressional approval the way the administration does will decide whether this arch is ever built.

We left out the dollar figure on purpose. Reports put the cost anywhere from over $100 million to $1 billion, and nobody has pinned it down.

posts.quote: TRUMP FIRED HIS CYBER CHIEF AFTER THE OUTAGES. WHY? "I DIDN'T THINK THAT PERSON WAS GOOD ENOUGH."
posts.alt: Photo-style AI image of a man in a navy suit at a podium, representing former National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Text below reads: Trump fired his cyber chief after the outages. Why? "I didn't think that person was good enough."
posts.caption:
President Trump has explained why his National Cyber Director is gone, and he did not soften it.

Asked why he fired Sean Cairncross, Trump said: "Because I didn't think that person was good enough." Cairncross took office August 4, 2025 and served about 15 months. Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies is now acting director.

The firing came after a rough stretch of tech outages that hit airports, banks and other systems. Trump rejected the idea that they added up to a pattern. "They were all separate events," he said.

Reports differed on whether Cairncross was pushed or left, and Fox News said the exact departure date was unclear. Trump's own answer settles the question of whether he was fired.
posts.first:
Cairncross was confirmed 59 to 35 in the Senate and was the President's top adviser on national cybersecurity strategy. Critics noted at his nomination that he came from the RNC and had little cyber experience.

Here is the part worth watching. Trump says the outages were separate events, yet he also fired the person in charge of defending against them. Both things can be true, but only one of them explains why the job suddenly opened.

Trump also asked Congress for $50 billion to modernize air traffic control. With the cyber director's chair now held by an acting official, the administration has a lot riding on getting the next pick right. The job exists to coordinate cybersecurity across federal agencies, so an empty chair during a run of outages is not a small thing. Whoever Trump names next will take over with the outage questions still unanswered and a $50 billion air traffic control request in front of Congress.
